# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** Associate
**Date:** November 10, 2026
**Re:** Laimul Baking Holdings, Inc. / Hearthline Bread Co.: post-closing exposure under the deal documents (ranked issues list)

---

## I. Background and Scope

Laimul Baking Holdings, Inc. ("**Laimul**" or "**Buyer**") bought all of the outstanding shares of Hearthline Bread Co. ("**Hearthline**" or the "**Company**") from Dekes Family Bakeries, LLC ("**Dekes**" or "**Seller**").

- **Signing and Closing.** The Stock Purchase Agreement ("**SPA**") was **signed and closed simultaneously on July 1, 2026** (SPA §3.1, the "Closing Date").
- **Purchase Price.** The price was $48,500,000 (SPA §2.1), paid as follows:
  - $38,150,000 in cash to Seller;
  - $3,600,000 into the Indemnity Escrow;
  - $750,000 into the Adjustment Escrow; and
  - a $6,000,000 subordinated Seller Note, issued by Laimul as Maker to Dekes as Holder (SPA §2.2).
- **Escrow.** The escrow is now governed by the Amended and Restated Escrow Agreement dated October 6, 2026, with Ashgrove Trust Company, N.A. as Escrow Agent.
- **Governing law.** All three deal documents are governed by Delaware law, with exclusive jurisdiction in the Court of Chancery (SPA §§11.6–11.7; Escrow §§6.2–6.3; Note §§9.6–9.7).

I reviewed all four files in the folder:

1. the SPA, including the Annex A Disclosure Schedule excerpts;
2. the A&R Escrow Agreement;
3. the Seller Promissory Note; and
4. the March 16, 2026 Mutual NDA.

The issues below are **ranked by commercial and legal consequence, with the most significant first**. Urgency of the deadline weighed heavily in the ranking. Assumptions are flagged in each issue and collected in Part IV.

## II. Summary Ranking

| Priority | Issue | Location | Key exposure | Deadline / urgency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | General reps, including food safety, expire six months after Closing, and claims are barred unless suit is filed | SPA §§9.1(a)(iii), 9.1(c), read with §1.1 ("Fundamental Representations") | Whole general-rep indemnity, including food safety, recall and Material Contracts reps | **January 1, 2027** (52 days away) |
| 2 | Pellucid change-of-control consent was never obtained | SPA Disclosure Schedule 4.9(a)(iii), read with Schedule 4.4 and SPA §§6.4, 7.2(c), 10.13 | Customer worth about 38% of net sales can terminate on 30 days' notice; indemnity recovery is doubtful | Live now |
| 3 | Working-capital Notice of Disagreement was four days late | Escrow Agreement Recitals C–D and §3.2; SPA §2.4(b)–(c) | $612,000 claimed shortfall; $750,000 Adjustment Escrow | Live now; Seller can serve a Release Demand at any time |
| 4 | Seller Note's narrow "Losses" definition defeats set-off for recall and similar losses | Note §4.2 and §1 ("Losses"), read with SPA §§1.1, 9.8, 11.9 | Set-off is unavailable for the most likely bakery losses; risk of a Note default if Laimul self-helps | Before the first set-off would be needed |
| 5 | Dekes can assign the Note to anyone, including a competitor, and the assignee receives customer-level data | Note §9.2, read with §6.1 | Competitor or allied investor gets monthly financials and customer pricing until 2030 | Ongoing; fix before any transfer |

---

## III. Issues

### Issue 1 — Indemnity survival gap: general representations, including food safety, expire January 1, 2027, and only a filed lawsuit preserves a claim

**Where it appears**

- SPA §1.1, definition of "Fundamental Representations."
- SPA §9.1(a)(iii) (survival periods).
- SPA §9.1(c) (claims bar).
- Related provisions: SPA §§9.4(a)–(b), 9.9.

**What the documents say**

- **Fundamental Representations are narrow.** Under §1.1 they are only §4.1 (Organization), §4.2 (Capitalization), §4.3 (Authority) and §4.20 (Brokers). **Section 4.15 (Food Safety; Product Recalls) is not a Fundamental Representation.** Neither is §4.9 (Material Contracts), §4.4 (Consents), §4.5 (Financial Statements), §4.10 (Customers) or §4.12 (Compliance).
- **General reps survive only six months.** Under §9.1(a)(iii), every representation other than the Fundamental Representations and §4.17 (Taxes) survives "until the date that is **six months after the Closing Date**." Measured from the July 1, 2026 Closing, that date is **January 1, 2027**.
- **Notice is not enough.** Section 9.1(c) bars any rep-and-warranty indemnity claim "unless the Indemnified Party has **commenced an Action** with respect to such claim in a court specified in Section 11.7" before the survival period expires. Unfiled claims are "forever barred."
  - A Claim Notice under §9.5, or a copy given to the Escrow Agent under Escrow §3.1(c), does not preserve a claim.
  - The parties expressly intend this to replace the statute of limitations, citing 10 Del. C. § 8106(c).

**Why it matters for Laimul**

- **The deadline is close.** Laimul has 52 days from today to discover, investigate and actually sue on any breach of the general reps.
- **Bakery problems surface slowly.** In a wholesale bakery, the most damaging problems tend to emerge months after closing, and many will not surface by January 1, 2027. Examples include:
  - undeclared allergens or cross-contact (FALCPA);
  - FDA Form 483 observations or warning letters following a routine inspection;
  - customer food-safety audit failures; and
  - recalls traceable to pre-Closing production.
- **Delaware will likely enforce the deadline.** Delaware courts generally enforce contractually shortened survival periods as limitations on when claims may be brought (see, e.g., *GRT, Inc. v. Marathon GTF Technology, Ltd.* (Del. Ch. 2011)). The §9.1(c) "commenced an Action" requirement is explicit. We should assume the court will apply it as written.
- **The escrow is the only backstop for general reps, and it may soon be released.**
  - Seller's liability for general reps is capped at the $3.6 million Indemnity Escrow Amount and is subject to a $363,750 deductible (§9.4(a)–(b)).
  - Section 9.9 requires a joint instruction to release the escrow within five Business Days after the survival date, less amounts claimed in Actions **then pending**.
  - If nothing is on file, Laimul loses its claims and must also instruct release of the $3.6 million.
- **The gap affects other issues in this memo.** Any indemnity theory relating to Pellucid (Issue 2), or recharacterizing the working-capital shortfall as a breach of the §4.5 financial statements rep (Issue 3), is also subject to this deadline.

**Assumption flagged:** January 1, 2027 is a Friday and a bank holiday. SPA §10.3 says that a period ending on a non-Business Day runs to the next Business Day, which would be Monday, January 4, 2027. However, §9.1(a)(iii) is drafted as a fixed "date that is six months after," not a period "within which" an act is done. It is unclear whether §10.3 applies. **We should not rely on the extension.** Treat **Thursday, December 31, 2026** as the latest filing date, and aim earlier given court filing logistics.

**Recommended fix**

1. **Run an immediate post-closing diligence sweep** with Laimul and Hearthline operations, QA and finance. It should cover:
   - FDA and USDA inspection history and correspondence;
   - allergen labeling and changeover records;
   - customer audit reports (Pellucid in particular);
   - consumer complaints and hold or withdrawal logs;
   - Material Contract compliance; and
   - the financial statements underlying the working-capital dispute.
2. **Prepare a protective Chancery complaint** and calendar a filing by mid-December 2026 for any identified or reasonably suspected breach.
   - Plead the claims with enough specificity to satisfy §9.1(c) as to each claim.
   - Consider pleading known risk categories, but note that a court may not treat a generic placeholder claim as an Action "with respect to such claim."
3. **Seek a written amendment from Seller under §11.10 before the deadline.** The amendment should:
   - extend general-rep survival to at least 18–24 months, with longer survival for §4.15;
   - replace the "commenced an Action" requirement with a Claim Notice standard; and
   - make corresponding changes to the §9.9 escrow release.

   Seller has an incentive to agree, because it would avoid a protective lawsuit and could pair the amendment with the other fixes in this memo (see Part V). An agreed tolling or standstill agreement is a fallback.
4. **Do not sign any §9.9 joint release instruction** until claims are filed or survival is extended.

---

### Issue 2 — Pellucid Grocers change-of-control consent was triggered at Closing, never obtained, and is likely not indemnifiable

**Where it appears**

- SPA Disclosure Schedule 4.9(a)(iii), item 1.
- SPA Schedule 4.4 ("None.").
- Read with SPA §§4.4, 6.4, 7.2(c) and 10.13.

**What the documents say**

- **The consent requirement.** Schedule 4.9(a)(iii) lists Hearthline's Co-Manufacturing and Supply Agreement with Pellucid Grocers, Inc. It states that:
  - Pellucid accounted for **approximately 38% of the Company's net sales** in FY2025; and
  - Pellucid "may terminate the agreement on 30 days' notice if the Company undergoes a change of control **without Pellucid's prior written consent**."
- **The omission.** Schedule 4.4 (Consents; Non-Contravention) says "None."
- **Why the omission matters.** Both the consent covenant (§6.4) and the consent closing condition (§7.2(c)) reach only consents "set forth on Schedule 4.4." The Pellucid consent was therefore:
  - never a covenant Seller had to perform;
  - never a condition Buyer could insist on; and
  - not listed for the post-Closing efforts covenant in §6.4.
- **The trigger.** The July 1, 2026 sale of 100% of Hearthline's stock to Laimul is a change of control of the Company.

**Why it matters for Laimul**

- **Pellucid can walk on short notice.** Pellucid holds a live right to terminate on 30 days' notice.
  - Losing about 38% of net sales would be a severe hit to Hearthline's revenue, plant utilization and margins.
  - It would also call into question the valuation underlying the $48.5 million price.
- **The indemnity route is weak.**
  - A §4.4(c) breach claim faces SPA §10.13, which deems a disclosure in any schedule section disclosed for every Article 4 section to which its relevance is "reasonably apparent on the face of the disclosure."
  - The Schedule 4.9 entry expressly describes a change-of-control consent right. Its relevance to §4.4 is very likely "reasonably apparent," so it probably qualifies the §4.4 representation.
  - A §6.4 covenant claim fails because the consent was never on Schedule 4.4.
  - Any rep claim that does survive is subject to the January 1, 2027 survival and lawsuit requirement (Issue 1), the $363,750 deductible and the $3.6 million cap.
- **The termination right may not be time-limited.** Nothing in the folder suggests it lapses. We do not have the Pellucid agreement itself (see assumptions).

**Assumptions flagged:**

1. Nothing in the folder shows that Pellucid's consent or a waiver was obtained. I assume none was. **We need to confirm this with the client.** Note that NDA §7.2 barred Laimul from contacting Hearthline customers about the transaction without Dekes's consent before signing. This may explain why the point was not caught.
2. We are relying on Seller's summary of the Pellucid agreement in the schedule. Under SPA §10.9 that summary is qualified by the full contract, which was "made available" in the data room. We should obtain and review the full agreement for:
   - the definition of "change of control";
   - any exercise window or lapse of the termination right;
   - notice mechanics; and
   - whether Pellucid has already been notified.
3. I assume Pellucid has not yet sent a termination notice. If it has, §4.9(b) and §4.10 speak only as of July 1, 2026 and would not help unless notice predated Closing.

**Recommended fix**

1. **Approach Pellucid promptly.** The approach should be commercially led, with counsel support.
   - Seek a written consent to, or waiver of, the change of control, ideally with ratification effective as of July 1, 2026.
   - Consider whether a modest commercial concession is worth securing the relationship.
   - Coordinate messaging carefully, since raising the issue alerts Pellucid to its leverage.
2. **Press Dekes for a special indemnity** for Losses arising from any Pellucid termination or adverse renegotiation linked to the change of control. The special indemnity should:
   - be uncapped by the general-rep cap and free of the deductible;
   - survive for the life of Pellucid's termination right;
   - be backed by a holdback of part of the Indemnity Escrow; and
   - carry an express right of set-off against the Seller Note, using SPA-defined Losses (see Issue 4).
3. **Preserve claims in parallel.** As a protective step, include a §4.4 and §4.9 claim (and any fraud or knowledge-based theory, if the facts support it) in any pre-January 1, 2027 filing. We should be candid with the client that §10.13 makes the rep claim uphill.

---

### Issue 3 — Buyer's working-capital Notice of Disagreement was four days late

**Where it appears**

- A&R Escrow Agreement Recitals C, D and E, and §3.2.
- Read with SPA §2.4(b)–(c) and §10.3.

**What the documents say**

- **Delivery and deadline.**
  - Recital C states that Seller delivered its Closing Statement on **August 25, 2026**.
  - SPA §2.4(b) requires a Notice of Disagreement "within 30 days after Seller's delivery of the Closing Statement."
  - Excluding the reference date (§10.3), the 30-day window **closed on September 24, 2026**, a Thursday and a Business Day.
- **Late delivery.** Recital D states that Buyer delivered its dispute notice, asserting a **$612,000** shortfall against Target Net Working Capital, on **September 28, 2026**. That is four days late.
- **Consequence under the SPA.** Under SPA §2.4(c), if no timely Notice of Disagreement is delivered, "the Closing Statement and Seller's calculation of Closing Net Working Capital shall be **final and binding** on the parties."

**Why it matters for Laimul**

- **Seller has a strong lateness argument.** Section 2.4(c) is self-executing, so Seller can argue that its Closing Statement is final. That would:
  - defeat Laimul's $612,000 claim; and
  - entitle Seller to the **$750,000 Adjustment Escrow** under §2.4(e).
- **If Seller's figure is above target, Laimul could also owe money.** If Seller's own NWC figure exceeds Target, Laimul may owe Seller the excess, up to $750,000, under §2.4(e)(ii). (I have not seen Seller's figure; see assumptions.)
- **The Release Demand procedure creates a short deadline.**
  - Under Escrow §3.2(b), Seller may serve a Release Demand certifying that NWC "has been finally determined under Section 2.4."
  - Laimul then has only **ten Business Days** after the Escrow Agent's receipt to deliver an Objection Notice, or the Escrow Agent pays out.
  - The Escrow Agent's duties are ministerial, and it is not charged with knowledge of the SPA (Escrow §§4.1–4.2).
- **The point has not been waived.** Recital E records that "no Party has accepted the Closing Statement" and that Buyer reserves all rights. Laimul has not acquiesced in Seller's position. However, §2.4(c) does not require acceptance, so the reservation does not cure the lateness.
- **Recasting the shortfall as an indemnity claim is difficult.**
  - Section 9.10 carves §2.4 disputes out of the exclusive indemnity remedy.
  - Recasting the shortfall as a §4.5 financial-statement breach would face anti-double-dip and "final and binding" arguments.
  - Any such claim would also be subject to the January 1, 2027 deadline (Issue 1).

**Assumptions flagged:**

1. I have taken the dates in Recitals C and D as accurate. The client should confirm:
   - the actual time and method of delivery of the Closing Statement under SPA §11.2;
   - the delivery of the Buyer Dispute Notice; and
   - whether any earlier written communication, before September 24, set out disputed items "in reasonable detail" and could itself qualify as a Notice of Disagreement.
2. I have not seen the Closing Statement or Seller's NWC figure.

**Available arguments, which are not strong on their own:**

- **Supporting documentation.** If the August 25 statement lacked the "reasonable supporting documentation" required by §2.4(a), Laimul can argue the clock never started. The same argument applies if Seller withheld access to records.
- **Waiver or estoppel.** Seller signed the A&R Escrow Agreement on October 6 reciting the dispute without asserting lateness. That supports waiver and estoppel arguments. Note, however, that SPA §11.10 requires waivers to be in a signed writing.

**Recommended fix**

1. **Before giving any joint release instruction, obtain Seller's written waiver** of the timeliness objection, or a written extension of the §2.4(b) deadline to September 28, 2026, under SPA §11.10. Ideally this would be part of a broader amendment package (see Part V).
2. **Do not sign any Joint Written Instruction for the Adjustment Escrow** until the timeliness point is resolved.
3. **Calendar a ten-Business-Day response protocol** so that any Release Demand is met with a timely Objection Notice under Escrow §3.2(b).
4. **Develop timeliness and estoppel arguments now**, using delivery records, the completeness of the supporting documentation and Seller's October 6 conduct. These would support a Chancery action if Seller refuses to waive.

---

### Issue 4 — The Seller Note's narrower "Losses" definition governs set-off and excludes recall, attorneys' fees and diminution in value

**Where it appears**

- Seller Note §4.2 (Set-Off) and §1 (definition of "Losses").
- Read with SPA §1.1 ("Losses"), §9.7, §9.8 and §11.9.

**What the documents say**

- **The SPA appears to give a broad set-off right.**
  - SPA §9.8 lets Buyer set off "any amount of Losses" to which a Buyer Indemnitee is entitled against amounts due under the Seller Note.
  - SPA §1.1 defines Losses broadly, "including reasonable attorneys' fees, diminution in value and **product withdrawal or recall** costs."
- **The Note narrows it.**
  - Note §4.2 limits set-off to "Losses (**as defined in this Note**)."
  - Note §1 defines Losses as out-of-pocket amounts "actually paid … to a Person other than Maker, the Company or any of their Affiliates, **excluding attorneys' fees, diminution in value, consequential damages and costs of any product withdrawal or recall**."
- **The SPA's precedence clause does not help.** SPA §11.9 normally makes the SPA prevail over Ancillary Agreements. However, it expressly provides that "the Seller Note shall control with respect to its own payment, **set-off** and acceleration terms." The Note's narrower definition therefore controls.

**Why it matters for Laimul**

- **The most likely losses cannot be set off.** For a bakery buyer, the most likely indemnifiable losses are recall and withdrawal costs, legal fees and value impairment. These are exactly the categories carved out.
- **Many direct losses are also excluded.** The "paid to a Person other than … the Company" limitation arguably excludes Hearthline's own internal costs, such as destroyed inventory, lost production and remediation by its own staff, even where they are not formally "recall" costs.
- **Laimul must keep paying Dekes while it pursues these claims.** The payments at stake are:
  - quarterly interest at 6% (Note §2.2); and
  - $1.5 million annual principal installments beginning July 1, 2027 (Note §2.1).

  Meanwhile, Laimul would have to pursue Dekes directly once the Indemnity Escrow is exhausted, since SPA §9.7 and Note §4.2 require recourse to the escrow first.
- **Self-help is dangerous.** If Laimul withholds payments on the strength of the SPA definition, it risks:
  - a payment Event of Default under Note §7.1(a);
  - Default Rate interest (§2.3);
  - acceleration (§7.2); and
  - collection costs (§7.4).

**Recommended fix**

1. **Amend the Note under Note §9.5 to conform the definition.** Revise Note §4.2 and §1 so that set-off is available for "Losses" as defined in the SPA (or delete the Note definition of Losses altogether).
2. **Confirm in the amendment that set-off covers the right claims.** Set-off should extend to any Pellucid special indemnity (Issue 2) and to amounts claimed in pending Actions, through a withholding or escrow-of-payments mechanism.
3. **Advise the client in the meantime** not to exercise set-off beyond the Note's definition. Any set-off should comply strictly with the ten-Business-Day notice requirement in §4.2.

---

### Issue 5 — Dekes may assign the Seller Note to anyone, including a competitor, who would then receive Laimul's financials and customer-level sales data

**Where it appears**

- Seller Note §9.2 (Assignment and Transfer).
- Read with Note §6.1 (Financial Information and Access).

**What the documents say**

- **Holder can transfer freely.** Note §9.2 lets Holder assign or transfer the Note "in whole or in part, to any Person **without the consent of Maker**," on notice only. Each assignee "succeeds to all rights of Holder." Maker, by contrast, cannot assign without Holder's consent.
- **Holder receives extensive information.** While any principal is outstanding, which could be until July 1, 2030, Note §6.1 requires Maker to deliver:
  - monthly consolidated financial statements;
  - **customer-level sales reports** showing net sales, unit volumes and average net pricing by customer and product category;
  - annual audited financials; and
  - access to the books, records and personnel of Laimul and Hearthline.

**Why it matters for Laimul**

- **Competitive data could reach a rival.** Dekes could sell the Note to a competing commercial bakery, or to a distressed-debt investor aligned with one. That buyer would receive Hearthline's customer-by-customer pricing and volume data, including for Pellucid, every month for up to four years.
- **No other document restricts the assignee.**
  - The confidentiality covenant (SPA §6.1) binds only Seller and its Affiliates.
  - The non-compete (SPA §6.2) binds only Seller and its Affiliates.
  - The NDA covers information exchanged "in connection with the Transaction," expires March 16, 2028, and does not cover post-Closing Note reporting.
  - Nothing in the SPA limits transfer of the Note.
- **The information covenant carries default risk.** Refusing to deliver the reports to an assignee would breach §6.1. After 30 days' notice, that becomes an Event of Default under §7.1(b), exposing Laimul to acceleration.

**Assumption flagged:** The Note does not say whether Maker's set-off rights under §4.2 survive against an assignee. Section 9.2 gives the assignee "all rights of Holder" but does not expressly say it takes subject to Maker's defenses and set-off. I assume a Delaware court would likely apply ordinary assignee-takes-subject-to-defenses principles. This should not be left to inference.

**Recommended fix**

1. **Restrict transfer.** Amend Note §9.2 to:
   - require Maker's prior written consent to any transfer (not to be unreasonably withheld for transfers to institutional lenders); and
   - in all events bar transfers to Competitors, their Affiliates and funds or investors holding interests in Competitors, with "Competitor" defined by reference to the SPA §6.2 business.
2. **Condition any permitted transfer** on:
   - the assignee's written joinder to a confidentiality undertaking; and
   - express confirmation that the assignee takes subject to Maker's set-off rights and defenses.
3. **Narrow the information rights in Note §6.1.**
   - Replace customer-level reports with aggregate or category-level reporting, or limit them to a clean-team or outside-advisor recipient (mirroring NDA §3.5).
   - Make the information rights personal to Dekes and non-transferable.
   - Add a confidentiality covenant within the Note itself.

---

## IV. Consolidated Assumptions and Open Items

1. **Survival date computation (Issue 1).** I treat the survival date as January 1, 2027. I do not rely on SPA §10.3 to extend it to January 4, 2027. Any filing should be made by December 31, 2026 at the latest.
2. **Pellucid consent (Issue 2).** I assume:
   - no consent or waiver was obtained;
   - no termination notice has been received; and
   - Schedule 4.9(a)(iii) accurately summarizes the Pellucid agreement.

   The full agreement is not in the folder and must be obtained.
3. **Working-capital dates (Issue 3).** I accept the August 25 and September 28, 2026 dates in the Escrow recitals. I have not seen Seller's Closing Statement, its NWC figure or its supporting documentation.
4. **Original Escrow Agreement.** It is not in the folder. I assume the A&R Escrow Agreement supersedes it entirely (Escrow §6.7).
5. **Senior Debt.** The Note is subordinated to "Senior Debt" (Note §5). I have not seen any Laimul credit agreement. If one exists, it may itself restrict Note amendments, which affects the fixes for Issues 4 and 5.
6. **Facts about the Business.** I have no information about any food-safety, FDA or customer-audit events since Closing. Issue 1 is ranked first because of its deadline and the breadth of rights at stake, not because a known breach has been identified.

## V. Other Observations

- **Mutual NDA (March 16, 2026).** I reviewed it. It does not create material post-closing exposure for Laimul.
  - Its customer non-contact covenant (§7.2) and employee non-solicit (§7.1) are effectively moot now that Laimul owns Hearthline. Both lapse no later than March 16, 2027 in any event.
  - Its only relevance is contextual: it explains why Laimul could not have verified Pellucid's position before signing (Issue 2), and its clean-team concept (§3.5) is a useful model for the Issue 5 fix.
  - Note that the NDA characterizes Hearthline information as "Confidential Information of Dekes." That characterization is anomalous after Closing and could be tidied up in any amendment package.
- **Cap and deductible.** General-rep recovery is capped at the $3.6 million escrow, with a $363,750 deductible (SPA §9.4). The client should understand that, even with an extended survival period, general-rep protection is modest relative to a $48.5 million deal.

## VI. Recommended Next Steps

1. **This week.**
   - Launch the diligence sweep and begin drafting the protective Chancery complaint (Issue 1).
   - Confirm the Pellucid facts and obtain the full Pellucid agreement (Issue 2).
   - Put a Release Demand response protocol in place with the client's General Counsel (Issue 3).
2. **Within two weeks.** Present Dekes with a **single written amendment package** under SPA §11.10 and Note §9.5, covering:
   - extended survival and replacement of the "commenced an Action" requirement with a Claim Notice standard;
   - a Pellucid special indemnity with a holdback and set-off;
   - a written waiver of the Notice of Disagreement timeliness objection;
   - conforming the Note's definition of Losses to the SPA definition; and
   - Note transfer and information restrictions.

   Dekes's leverage points are the escrow releases and its interest in avoiding litigation.
3. **No later than mid-December 2026.** If the amendment is not signed, file the protective Chancery action covering all identified or suspected general-rep claims, including Pellucid. Withhold any §9.9 release instruction.

I am happy to prepare the amendment term sheet and a draft complaint outline on your instruction.

## III. Discussion

### Issue 1: Indemnity Survival Gap. General Representations, Including Food Safety, Expire About January 1, 2027, and Only a Filed Lawsuit Preserves a Claim

**Where it appears**

SPA §9.1(a)(iii) and §9.1(c), read together with the definition of "Fundamental Representations" in SPA §1.1.

**What the documents say**

- **Fundamental Representations are narrow.** SPA §1.1 limits them to four sections: §4.1 (Organization), §4.2 (Capitalization), §4.3 (Authority) and §4.20 (Brokers). Under §9.1(a), Fundamental Representations and the §4.17 Tax representation survive until 60 days after the applicable statute of limitations.
- **Everything else is a general representation.** All other representations survive only "until the date that is six months after the Closing Date" (§9.1(a)(iii)). That category includes:
  - §4.15 (Food Safety; Product Recalls);
  - §4.9 (Material Contracts);
  - §4.4 (Consents);
  - §4.5 (Financial Statements);
  - §4.12 (Compliance with Laws); and
  - §4.10 (Customers and Suppliers).
- **The food safety representation is not fundamental.** It does not receive extended survival.
- **A Claim Notice is not enough.** Under §9.1(c), no claim under §9.2(a) "may be brought or maintained unless the Indemnified Party has **commenced an Action** with respect to such claim in a court specified in Section 11.7 before the expiration of the applicable survival period." Any claim not so commenced is "forever barred." A Claim Notice under §9.5 does not preserve a claim.
- **The parties chose this result deliberately.** Section 9.1(c) expressly invokes 10 Del. C. § 8106(c). Delaware courts enforce contractually shortened survival periods of this kind as limitations periods. We should expect the provision to be enforced as written.
- **Recovery for general reps is also capped.** Seller's liability for these representations is limited to the $3,600,000 Indemnity Escrow Amount (§9.4(b)) and applies only above a $363,750 Deductible (§9.4(a)). Fraud is excluded from these limits (§9.4(d)).

**The deadline**

Six months after July 1, 2026 is **January 1, 2027**.

> **Assumption flagged:** January 1, 2027 is a Friday and New Year's Day, which is not a Business Day. SPA §10.3 provides that if "the last day of a period is not a Business Day, the period ends on the next Business Day." That could extend the deadline to **Monday, January 4, 2027**. It is not clear that §10.3 applies to a survival date expressed as "the date that is six months after the Closing Date," rather than to a period "within which… any act is to be done." Seller would argue it does not. **We should treat December 31, 2026 as the operative last day for filing** and not rely on any rollover.

**Why it matters for Laimul**

- **Laimul has had the business for only about four months.** For a wholesale bakery, the most likely indemnifiable problems surface on a lag. These include:
  - undeclared major allergens or labeling non-compliance under FALCPA and the FD&C Act;
  - historic FDA Form 483 observations;
  - customer food-safety audit failures; and
  - latent recall triggers.
- **Problems that surface after January 1, 2027 are unrecoverable.** Any problem arising from pre-closing conduct that emerges after that date cannot be recovered under the general representations, except through a fraud claim.
- **Even known problems require litigation now.** Laimul must actually file suit in Delaware by year-end. Sending a notice will not preserve the claim.
- **The escrow will be released.** Under SPA §9.9 and Escrow Agreement §3.1(b), the parties must jointly instruct release of the entire $3.6M Indemnity Escrow within five Business Days after the survival period expires. The only exception is amounts claimed in Actions then pending. Without a filed Action, Laimul loses its primary source of recovery.
- **In practice, the indemnity protection for operational representations is largely illusory** unless we act now.

**Recommended fix**

1. **Accelerated post-closing diligence.** Immediately commission a focused review of:
   - allergen labeling and declarations;
   - FDA/USDA inspection history;
   - customer audit reports, especially Pellucid's;
   - supplier allergen certificates;
   - complaint and stock-recovery logs; and
   - pre-closing financial statements and working-capital accounts.
   
   Target completion by early December 2026.
2. **Protective filing.** Prepare to file a complaint in the Court of Chancery before December 31, 2026 on any identified or reasonably suspected breach, including the Pellucid issue (Issue 2), to the extent viable. Also deliver contemporaneous Claim Notices and copy the Escrow Agent (Escrow Agreement §3.1(c)).
3. **Seek an amendment or tolling agreement.** Approach Dekes for a written amendment under SPA §11.10 that:
   - extends general survival to at least 18–24 months; and
   - extends §4.15 (Food Safety) survival to the statute of limitations, or treats §4.15 as a Fundamental Representation.
   
   At a minimum, seek a tolling agreement that substitutes a Claim Notice for the "commenced an Action" requirement. We have leverage: Dekes wants the Indemnity Escrow released, and it wants clean Note payments.
4. **Escrow release.** Do not sign any Joint Written Instruction releasing the Indemnity Escrow until the above is resolved.
5. **Fraud review.** Preserve and review diligence materials for potential fraud claims, which fall outside the §9.4 limits. (Note also that the §9.10 exclusive-remedy clause carves out fraud.)

### Issue 2: Pellucid Grocers Change-of-Control Consent Was Triggered at Closing but Never Obtained

**Where it appears**

SPA Disclosure Schedule 4.9(a)(iii), item 1, read against Schedule 4.4 ("None"), SPA §6.4 (Third-Party Consents), §7.2(c) (consent closing condition) and §10.13 (Cross-Disclosure).

**What the documents say**

- **The disclosure.** Schedule 4.9(a)(iii) discloses Hearthline's Co-Manufacturing and Supply Agreement with Pellucid Grocers, Inc. It states that Pellucid accounted for approximately **38% of Hearthline's net sales** in FY2025 and that Pellucid "may terminate the agreement on 30 days' notice if the Company undergoes a change of control **without Pellucid's prior written consent**."
- **The consent schedule is blank.** Schedule 4.4 (Consents; Non-Contravention) reads simply "None."
- **No covenant or closing condition covered Pellucid.** Seller's consent covenant (§6.4) and Buyer's closing condition (§7.2(c)) each reach only consents "set forth on Schedule 4.4." Because Pellucid was not listed, Seller had no obligation to seek its consent, and the closing condition did not cover it.
- **The trigger has occurred.** The sale of 100% of Hearthline's stock to Laimul on July 1, 2026 is a change of control of the Company.
- **No consent appears in the file.** Nothing in the matter folder indicates that Pellucid consented.

> **Assumption flagged:** I have not seen the Pellucid agreement itself. The Disclosure Schedule summary is "qualified by reference to the full text" (SPA §10.9). I am assuming the summary is accurate, and that the termination right is not time-limited (for example, exercisable only within a set window after the change of control). I am also assuming no consent or waiver was obtained outside the documents I reviewed. We should confirm all three points with the client and obtain the contract.

**Why it matters for Laimul**

- **Pellucid holds a live, unconditional termination right.** It can exercise that right on 30 days' notice over roughly 38% of the acquired revenue base. This is the most significant commercial exposure in the deal. Pellucid can also use the right as leverage to reprice the private-label program.
- **Indemnity recovery is doubtful.**
  - A claim that §4.4(c) was breached is the obvious route, because the transaction did "give rise to [a] right of termination" under a Material Contract and Schedule 4.4 said "None." However, §10.13 deems any matter disclosed in one schedule section disclosed for every other Article 4 section where its relevance is "reasonably apparent on the face of the disclosure." The Schedule 4.9 language expressly describes a change-of-control termination right. Seller will argue its relevance to §4.4 is facially apparent, which would defeat the claim.
  - No covenant claim exists under §6.4, because the consent was never scheduled.
  - Any representation claim is a general-representation claim. It is therefore subject to the January 1, 2027 file-suit deadline, the Deductible, and the $3.6M cap (see Issue 1). The cap is small relative to the value of a 38% customer.

**Recommended fix**

1. **Approach Pellucid immediately.** Obtain the full Pellucid agreement and confirm the terms. Then seek Pellucid's written consent to the change of control, or a written waiver of the termination right, in coordination with Hearthline's commercial team. Consider whether modest commercial concessions are worth offering to secure a clean waiver.
2. **Press Seller for a special indemnity.** Seek a negotiated special indemnity from Dekes for losses from any Pellucid termination or repricing tied to the change of control. It should:
   - sit outside the Deductible and cap;
   - be backed by a holdback of part of the Indemnity Escrow beyond the January 1, 2027 release date; and
   - provide express set-off rights against the Note, using a conformed definition of Losses (see Issue 3).
3. **Preserve the claim.** File a protective claim under §4.4 (and potentially §4.9(b) and §4.10) before the survival deadline. We should acknowledge internally that §10.13 makes success uncertain.
4. **Check the NDA point.** See Issue 5 regarding the NDA customer-contact restriction, which I do not believe bars this outreach post-closing but which should be cleared.

### Issue 3: The Note's Narrow "Losses" Definition Defeats Set-Off for Recall, Allergen and Legal Costs

**Where it appears**

Note §4.2 (Set-Off) and Note §1 (definition of "Losses"), read against SPA §1.1 (definition of "Losses"), §9.8 (Right of Set-Off), §9.7 (Order of Recovery) and §11.9 (Order of Precedence).

**What the documents say**

- **The SPA grants broad set-off.** SPA §9.8 lets Buyer set off "any amount of Losses" to which a Buyer Indemnitee is entitled against amounts payable under the Note. SPA §1.1 defines Losses broadly to include "reasonable attorneys' fees, diminution in value and product withdrawal or recall costs."
- **The Note uses its own, narrower definition.** Note §4.2 permits set-off only of "Losses (**as defined in this Note**)." Note §1 defines that term as out-of-pocket amounts actually paid to unaffiliated third parties, "**excluding attorneys' fees**, diminution in value, consequential damages and costs of any **product withdrawal or recall**."
- **The order-of-precedence clause does not help.** SPA §11.9 normally makes the SPA prevail over Ancillary Agreements. It contains a proviso, however, that "the Seller Note shall control with respect to its own payment, **set-off** and acceleration terms." On set-off, the Note's narrower definition therefore governs.

**Why it matters for Laimul**

- **The most likely bakery losses cannot be withheld.** The losses a bakery acquirer is most likely to suffer are recall and withdrawal costs, lost value from an allergen event, and legal fees. Precisely these cannot be withheld from Note payments.
- **Laimul must keep paying Dekes while pursuing claims.** It must continue paying 6% interest quarterly and $1.5M principal installments starting July 1, 2027, and pursue those Losses directly against Dekes.
- **Dekes's creditworthiness after closing is unknown.** This matters most once the Indemnity Escrow is exhausted or released, because the escrow is first in the §9.7 order of recovery and set-off is second.
- **Withholding carries default risk.** If Laimul withholds amounts that do not fit the Note definition, it risks an Event of Default under Note §7.1(a). That could expose it to Default Rate interest (§2.3), acceleration (§7.2(b)) and collection costs (§7.4).

**Recommended fix**

1. **Amend the Note** under Note §9.5 so that, for purposes of §4.2, "Losses" means Losses as defined in the SPA. Alternatively, delete the Note's §1 definition and conform §4.2 to SPA §9.8.
2. **Package with Issue 1.** Pair this request with the survival and Pellucid negotiations as a single post-closing "clean-up" amendment.
3. **Instruct the client in the meantime.** Advise the client not to set off any recall, legal-fee or diminution amounts against Note payments without our sign-off. Any proper set-off requires 10 Business Days' prior written notice identifying the related Claim Notice (Note §4.2).

### Issue 4: The Note Is Freely Assignable, Including to a Competitor, Who Would Receive Laimul's Customer-Level Sales Data

**Where it appears**

Note §9.2 (Assignment and Transfer), read with Note §6.1 (Financial Information and Access).

**What the documents say**

- **Dekes can transfer the Note to anyone.** Note §9.2 permits Holder to "assign or transfer this Note, in whole or in part, to any Person **without the consent of Maker**," on mere notice. Each assignee "succeeds to all rights of Holder."
- **The restriction runs one way.** Laimul may not assign without Holder's consent.
- **Information rights travel with the Note.** Note §6.1 requires Laimul, while any principal is outstanding (through July 1, 2030), to deliver:
  - monthly consolidated financial statements (§6.1(a));
  - **monthly customer-level sales reports showing net sales, unit volumes and average net pricing by customer and product category** (§6.1(b));
  - annual audited financials (§6.1(c)); and
  - access to books, records and personnel on five Business Days' notice (§6.1(d)).
- **The SPA does not restrict transfer.** SPA §11.4 restricts assignment of the SPA, not of the Note. SPA §6.1 binds only Seller and its Affiliates. Seller's non-compete (SPA §6.2) does not bind an unaffiliated transferee.

**Why it matters for Laimul**

- **A competitor could buy the Note.** Dekes could sell the Note, or a participation in it, to a competing commercial wholesale bakery or a fund allied with one. That transferee would then obtain monthly, customer-by-customer pricing and volume data on Hearthline's accounts, including Pellucid, for up to four years.
- **This is a competitive and antitrust problem.** It is precisely the competitively sensitive information that the NDA's §3.5 "Clean Team" protocol was designed to wall off during diligence.
- **Laimul would have no confidentiality protection.** The Note has no confidentiality covenant binding the Holder or its assigns.

**Recommended fix**

1. **Amend Note §9.2** to require Maker's prior written consent to any assignment or participation. At a minimum, it should flatly **bar transfers to competitors** of Laimul or Hearthline, and to their Affiliates and funds, with any non-consensual transfer void.
2. **Narrow Note §6.1.** Limit information rights to:
   - quarterly consolidated financials;
   - deletion of §6.1(b) customer-level reporting, or substitution of aggregated data;
   - restriction of §6.1(d) access to the period while an Event of Default is continuing; and
   - a confidentiality undertaking binding Holder and every permitted assignee.
3. **Consider prepayment.** If Dekes resists, Note §3.1 permits prepayment without premium. Partial prepayment, or a refinancing that takes out the Note, eliminates the exposure. This should be weighed against the loss of set-off capacity (Issue 3).

### Issue 5: Mutual NDA. No Material Exposure; Two Residual Points

**Where it appears**

NDA §§1.1, 7.2 and 8.1.

**Assessment**

The NDA was a pre-signing evaluation agreement and is largely superseded in practice by the SPA. I do not see material exposure for Laimul. Two points warrant brief attention:

- **Customer-contact restriction (§7.2).** Until the earlier of termination of discussions and March 16, 2027, Laimul may not initiate contact with Hearthline customers "concerning the Transaction or Hearthline's business" without Dekes's consent.
  > **Assumption flagged:** I read this restriction as having lapsed in substance at Closing. Discussions culminated in a definitive agreement, and post-closing contacts by Hearthline's owner with Hearthline's own customers are ordinary-course business. The NDA does not expressly terminate on closing, however. Before Laimul approaches Pellucid about consent (Issue 2), we should obtain a short written acknowledgment from Dekes that §7.2 no longer applies, or address it in the clean-up amendment.
- **Ownership of Hearthline information (§1.1).** The NDA treats Hearthline information as "Confidential Information of Dekes." It remains in effect until March 16, 2028 (§8.1), with indefinite protection for trade secrets such as recipes and formulations. Post-closing, this is anomalous because Laimul now owns that information. The amendment should confirm that the NDA imposes no restriction on Laimul's use of Hearthline information. Seller's post-closing confidentiality obligation under SPA §6.1 runs in Laimul's favor and should be the operative provision.

**Recommended fix:** Include a short NDA termination or acknowledgment in the clean-up amendment package.

## IV. Escrow Agreement: Other Observations

Apart from its interaction with Issue 1, I did not identify separate structural exposure in the Escrow Agreement. Two points to keep in view:

- **Indemnity Escrow release timing.** The release is tied directly to SPA §9.9 (Escrow Agreement §3.1(b)). Laimul should not execute any Joint Written Instructions for the Indemnity Escrow until the survival and Pellucid issues are resolved or Actions are on file.
- **Unilateral Release Demands.** Escrow Agreement §3.2(b) permits either Party to make a unilateral Release Demand on the Adjustment Escrow. Silence for ten Business Days results in disbursement. The client should designate a responsible officer to monitor and respond to any Release Demand promptly.
